prompt.context: Our client is a large car manufacturer that has been facing financial stress for the past few years. To overcome this crisis, they bought a small bank and started offering a lease at a lower rate than the other car manufacturers. This move has positioned our client strategically in the market and has helped them regain market share. However, the problem they are facing now is that customers are complaining of poor customer service in the banking division. The client reached us to help them improve their banking division customer service. In particular, they want to create a call center to provide support to all lease customers, but they don't know how big this call center should be.
prompt.question: How many employees do they need to hire for this call center?

clarifying_info.q: Does the bank offer leases for other manufacturers' cars as well?
clarifying_info.a: No. The bank offers the lease only for cars from its parent company.

clarifying_info.q: Does the call center also handle prospective customers?
clarifying_info.a: No. The call center is focused only on clients that have already signed the lease contract. It does not attend to prospective customers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of the US?
What age range buys new cars?
What is the life expectancy in the US and how is the population distributed?
clarifying_info.a: Life expectancy is 80 years and the population is uniformly distributed among all ages.

clarifying_info.q: What fraction of the population is willing to buy new cars?
clarifying_info.a: With the current crisis, only 50% of the population is willing to buy new cars. The remainder prefers to buy used cars.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average lifetime of a car?
What is the client's market share?
What fraction of the client's customers use the lease?
clarifying_info.a: 40% of the client's customers use the lease to acquire the car.

clarifying_info.q: How often do customers call the call center?
clarifying_info.a: The client expects that customers will call the call center only once a year until the end of the lease contract.

clarifying_info.q: Are calls uniformly distributed throughout the year and day?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. You can assume all calls are uniformly distributed throughout the year and during the day — no peak periods.

clarifying_info.q: What are the call center hours of operation?
clarifying_info.a: The call center receives calls only from 8am to 8pm, Monday to Sunday.

clarifying_info.q: How many hours/days can employees work?
clarifying_info.a: The union contract states that employees can only work 6 hours per day, 6 days per week.

clarifying_info.q: How long is the average call?
clarifying_info.a: On average, each call is 5 minutes long.

clarifying_info.q: How many days are in a year for this calculation?

framework: Car Leases: estimate the pool of active lease customers — client's share of the US car market, fraction of buyers who lease vs. buy, and length of the lease
Call Center Demand: translate active lease customers into annual calls, then into daily call volume and total minutes of demand
Call Center Supply: convert daily demand into headcount — hours each employee can work per day, days per week, and call center operating hours
Adjust for scheduling constraints: the call center is open 7 days but employees work only 6 days per week, so a staffing uplift is required

questions.prompt: Estimate the number of cars sold in the US per year.
questions.guidance: Use a population segmentation approach: start with total US population, isolate the age cohort that buys new cars (20–60 out of 80-year lifespan = 50%), apply the share willing to buy new vs. used (50%), then divide by the average car lifetime to get annual purchases.

math.setup: Cars sold in US = (Population × fraction in buying age range × fraction willing to buy new) / average car lifetime
steps: Fraction willing to buy new cars = 50%
Cars sold per year = 75M / 5 years = 15M cars/year

questions.prompt: How many of the client's customers sign a lease each year?
questions.guidance: Apply the client's market share to total market sales, then apply the lease take-rate.

math.setup: Lease customers per year = cars sold in US × client market share × lease fraction

questions.prompt: How many calls does the call center receive per year, and per day?
questions.guidance: Each lease lasts 3 years and customers call once per year, so every new lease customer generates 3 calls over the life of the contract. Divide total annual calls by 360 to get daily volume.

math.setup: Total annual calls = new lease customers/year × lease length (years). Calls per day = total annual calls / 360.
math.answer: 1.8 million calls per year; 5,000 calls per day

questions.prompt: How many employees does the call center need to handle daily demand?
questions.guidance: Convert daily call volume to total minutes of demand, then divide by minutes each employee can work per operating day. Finally, adjust for the 7-days-open vs. 6-days-worked mismatch.

math.setup: Step 1 — employees for a single operating day: demand (minutes) / (employee hours/day × 60). Step 2 — staffing uplift: call center is open 7 days/week but employees work 6 days/week, so multiply by 7/6.
steps: Daily demand in minutes = 5,000 calls × 5 min/call = 25,000 minutes
Minutes an employee works per day = 6 hours × 60 min/hr = 360 minutes
Employees needed for one day = 25,000 / 360 ≈ 69.4 → round to 70
Staffing uplift for 7-day operation with 6-day employees: 70 × (7/6) = 70 + 70 × (1/6) ≈ 70 + 11.7 ≈ 82 employees

brainstorming.prompt: The client does not have enough money in their budget to hire all 82 employees. What would you suggest to reduce the number of employees?

categories.name: Reduce number of calls
ideas: Develop a customer-facing website that easily provides information directly, reducing the need to call
Map the most common questions and publish a FAQ on the customer website
Offer an alternative communication channel (e.g., live chat) that can handle more volume at lower per-contact cost

categories.name: Reduce average call length
ideas: Invest in voice recognition technology to faster identify the customer's problem before directing them to an operator
Train employees more thoroughly so they can resolve issues faster
Create decision-tree scripts or knowledge-base tools for agents to look up answers quickly

recommendation: The client needs approximately 82 employees to fully staff the call center under current assumptions
If budget does not allow full staffing, prioritize self-service digital channels (FAQ/website) to deflect the most common inquiries, which directly reduces required headcount
risks: Call volume could be higher than modeled if customers call more than once per year or if the lease portfolio grows faster than projected
Union constraints (6 hours/day, 6 days/week) limit scheduling flexibility; any changes to operating hours would require renegotiation
next_steps: Pilot the call center with a smaller team while rolling out a self-service website to measure actual call deflection rates
Track call reason codes from day one to identify the top categories for FAQ development
Revisit headcount after 6 months of data on actual call frequency and duration
